title: How many in total?
keyIdea: The last number you say when counting tells you how many there are.

kid: When you finish counting, the last number you said tells you how many there are altogether.
It doesn't matter which object you start with, or how the objects are arranged. A line of 6 and a messy pile of 6 are both 6.
adult: This is the cardinality principle: the final number word names the size of the whole set. A child who recounts from one when asked 'how many?' can recite numbers but hasn't yet linked the last word to the total.
Two related facts: the order you count in doesn't change the total, and spreading out or bunching up the objects doesn't change it either.

familyTip: Ask 'so how many is that?' after counting. If your child starts again from one, count together and stress the last word.

practice.prompt: You count shells: 'one, two, three, four, five, six, seven.' How many shells are there?
practice.hint: Which number did you say last?
practice.explain: The last number said was seven, so there are 7 shells.

practice.prompt: 8 counters in a line are pushed together into a pile. How many counters are there now?
practice.hint: Did any counters get added or taken away?
practice.explain: Moving counters doesn't add or remove any, so there are still 8.

practice.hint: Count in a steady rhythm, one triangle per word.

practice.prompt: Lily counts some toys starting with the teddy and gets 6. Jo counts the same toys starting with the car. What should Jo get?
practice.hint: Does the starting point change how many toys there are?
practice.explain: The number of toys is the same whatever order you count them in, so Jo also gets 6.

items.prompt: After counting 'one, two, … nine', someone asks 'How many?' What is the best answer?
items.hint: The last number you said tells you.
items.explain: The last number word, nine, is the total.

items.hint: Count every star across all the groups.

items.prompt: Ten coins are spread out on a table. Another ten coins are stacked in a tower. Which has more coins?
items.hint: Count each set in your head.
items.explain: Both sets have ten coins; the arrangement doesn't change the number.
